title: Ten-Minute Stabilization Checklist and Customer Briefs
author: Maya Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document is a compact, prescriptive playbook for the first 10 minutes after an operational signal that materially affects customer experience. It combines a rapid-stabilization checklist, service-specific mitigations for common failure modes, a clear escalation ladder, and customer-facing status templates suitable for status.redwood.ai and enterprise communication. Use this when SLOs are at risk (see SLO section) or when an incident is declared.

Scope: Production services that impact hosted inference, Dedicated pools (redwood-dedicated-*), and Private control plane components. Not intended for minor developer-facing issues or backlog tasks.

Audience: On-call engineers, incident commanders, customer success, and on-call rotation leads.

Service ownership and SLOs

- Example services in scope:
  - redwood-serve-api (external REST/streaming gateway)
  - runtime-inference (GPU serving runtime pool)
  - kv-cache (Redis cluster used for prefix caching)
  - routing-proxy (smart-request-router)
- Key SLOs to watch (example thresholds):
  - Availability (p99 request success) target: 99.95% per region
  - Latency: p95 < 200ms, p99 < 600ms for small generation requests
  - Model Quality: less than 1% prompt-set regression alerts per deployment
  - Cost/Throughput: CPU/GPU saturation > 85% triggers scaling actions

Severity taxonomy (quick reference)

- Sev 1 (Critical): Global or multi-region outage or SLO breach > 30 minutes (customer-visible downtime). Examples: service returning 5xx for > 20% of requests for 5 minutes; routing-proxy down in all regions.
- Sev 2 (Major): Single-region outage or severe degradation affecting significant customer subsets. Examples: p99 latency spike > 2x SLO; KV cache > 90% eviction rate causing sustained latency increase.
- Sev 3 (Minor): Degradation limited to a small set of customers or graceful fallback working; local non-customer-facing incidents.

Ten-minute stabilization checklist (ordered tasks to run in the first 10 minutes)

0. Acknowledge and create the incident artifact (0:00 - 0:01)
  - Acknowledge page in PagerDuty/incident tool immediately.
  - Create a dedicated incident channel: #incident-<svc>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMM> (e.g. #incident-runtime-20260210-1023).
  - Start a shared document with timeline headers (minute marks).

1. Assign roles (0:00 - 0:02)
  - Incident Commander (IC): owns decisions, prioritization, and public messaging.
  - Service Owner / Primary on-call: subject-matter expert for impacted service.
  - Communications Lead: prepares status updates and liaises with CS.
  - Secondary on-call: escalated engineering support.

2. Initial triage (0:02 - 0:05) — rapid signal aggregation
  - Check global dashboards: grafana/redwood/global-slo, grafana/redwood/latency-p99, and redwood-alerts channel.
  - Query error rates and latency by region and by model (example query):
    - grafana query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="redwood-serve-api",status=~"5.."}[1m])) by (region)
  - Identify scope: all customers, specific customer IDs, or internal-only.
  - Check deployment activity in last 30 minutes: gitops status, CI/CD pipeline: ci/cd-runner -> last successful deploys to runtime-inference.

3. Immediate mitigation options (0:05 - 0:10) — pick the least-invasive that will restore customer experience
  - Fail open to fallback model: If routing-proxy can fall back to a smaller verified model variant (model-bundle-v1 -> model-bundle-fallback-v1), switch routing policy to fallback for impacted region.
  - Scale & restart: For GPU OOM or saturation, trigger scale-up: runbooks/commands:
    - kubectl -n production scale deployment runtime-inference --replicas=6
    - or trigger autoscaler: curl -X POST https://ops-api.redwood.internal/autoscaler/scale?pool=runtime-inference&delta=+2
  - Cache bypass: If kv-cache causing correctness or eviction storms, switch header X-Bypass-Cache: true at proxy for 10 minutes or flip feature flag: ff toggleset cache-bypass runtime-inference true
  - Traffic partition: Route a subset (10-20%) to Dedicated or a secondary region: routing-proxy route set --service runtime-inference --region eu-west-1 --weight 80 --backup us-west-2 20
  - Hot rollback: If a deploy in last 20 minutes correlates, initiate a rollback via ci/cd pipeline: ci rollback <pipeline-id>.
  - Controlled throttling: Apply rate-limits at edge to protect backend: edgectl set-rate-limit --service redwood-serve-api --qps 1000

4. Confirm stabilization (by minute 10)
  - Check that error-rate drops to below 5% of baseline or p99 latency returns to within 1.5x SLO for 5 consecutive minutes.
  - If not stabilized, IC escalates to full incident declaration and expands responders.

Service-specific quick mitigations (one-liners)

- runtime-inference (GPU OOM/saturation): restart affected pods, scale pool, reduce max sequence-length via request transform to limit tokens, switch to quantized model variant.
- kv-cache (Redis evictions / timeouts): increase read replicas, temporarily set prefix caching ttl to 30s, fail open to origin.
- redwood-serve-api (5xx from internal errors): toggle blue/green traffic to previous release, increase pod replicas, gather stack traces: kubectl logs -f deployment/redwood-serve-api -c api | grep ERROR -n 200
- routing-proxy (routing failures): restart routing-proxy instances in one AZ at a time; if config push failed, revert last config commit.

Escalation ladder and timeboxes

- 0m: acknowledge and assign roles.
- 3m: determine scope and impact (IC decision node).
- 10m: require an explicit stabilization action (see checklist). If unsuccessful, escalate to on-call rotation lead and SRE manager.
- 30m: involve Product (if customer-facing regression) and Customer Success for immediate customer outreach.
- 60m: consider executive notification if SLO breach persists or enterprise customers are severely impacted.

Customer-facing status templates (use these verbatim or adapt for tone)

- Initial acknowledgement (use within 10 minutes):
  Subject: Incident: {service} degraded in {region} — acknowledged
  Body:
  We are aware of an issue affecting {service} in {region}. Our on-call team has acknowledged the problem and is actively investigating. At this time:
  - Impact: {short statement of who/what is affected} 
  - Mitigation actions in progress: {eg. rolling restart / failover to fallback model / autoscaling}
  - Next update: within 15 minutes or sooner.

- 30-minute update (if not resolved):
  Subject: Update: {service} incident continuing — mitigation in progress
  Body:
  Status update at {time}:
  - Current impact and scope (updated)
  - Actions taken: {detailed bullet list of actions with timestamps}
  - Short-term plan: {what we will try next}
  - ETA for next update: 30 minutes

- Resolution notice (after service restored):
  Subject: Resolved: {service} incident in {region}
  Body:
  The incident affecting {service} in {region} has been resolved as of {time}. Summary:
  - Root cause (high-level): {brief RCA stub}
  - What we did to restore service: {list}
  - Next steps: full post-incident review scheduled; customers directly impacted will be contacted by Customer Success.

Internal incident timeline template (use in the incident doc)

- 00:00 — PagerDuty alert, IC acknowledged (who)
- 00:02 — First triage (who checked dashboards)
- 00:04 — Mitigation started (actions)
- 00:08 — Stabilization metrics observed (error-rate, latency)
- 00:12 — Decision: continue mitigation / expand incident

Postmortem and follow-up (post-incident checklist)

- Create postmortem within 72 hours. Must include:
  - Executive summary (2–3 sentences)
  - Chronology with minute resolution for first hour, 15-minute buckets after
  - Root cause analysis with evidence (logs, flamegraphs, kernel traces)
  - Corrective actions: short-term (within 7 days) and long-term (owner + timeline)
  - Measurement plan: how will we confirm the fix avoids regressions (synthetic tests, load tests, new alerts)
- Action ownership: assign Jira ticket(s) with clear owners and due dates.
- Postmortem review: schedule a 1-hour review with stakeholders within 7 days.

Runbook hygiene and game-day guidance

- Keep the most relevant runbook steps in the first 10 lines of the runbook (summary + 1-liner mitigations).
- Use canary test harnesses in the qa game-day environment before rolling fixes to production.
- Game-day checklist (preparation): verify shadowing oncall, ensure synthetic traffic generators are healthy, provision an observer channel for execs, prepare customer-facing snippets.

On-call rotation and handoff checklist

- Primary on-call: 7x24 coverage with 8-hour shifts is recommended for SMEs; for general SREs use 12-hour rotations depending on team capacity.
- Secondary on-call: follow-the-sun overlap windows (first 30 minutes of each shift) for knowledge transfer.
- Handoff checklist:
  - Confirm active incidents (none / list)
  - Review outstanding postmortem actions assigned to the oncall owner
  - Share sticky notes about recent deploys or planned maintenance
  - Ensure credentials and runbook links accessible

Evidence collection and runbook snippets to capture during incident

- Collect: stack traces, pprof, top-level flamegraphs, last 2000 lines of logs for affected pods, metrics snapshots (prometheus export), and PagerDuty timeline.
- Commands to run and capture output:
  - kubectl -n production get pods -o wide --selector=app=runtime-inference > pods.txt
  - kubectl -n production logs deployment/runtime-inference --since=15m > logs-15m.txt
  - redis-cli -h kv-cache.prod.internal INFO > redis-info.txt
  - perf top or pprof snapshot for heavy CPU profiles (if safe)

Special guidance for enterprise customers and private deployments

- If an incident impacts Dedicated or Private customers, Customer Success must be looped by minute 10. Use the enterprise template (append customer impact table) and enable a direct Slack or Zoom bridge with the customer success lead.
- For Private/VPC: coordinate with the Private Deployments on-call; do not access customer data without explicit authorization. Follow the Private incident response checklist (link in related pages).

Appendix: Example customer update (copy-paste friendly)

- Initial (10-minute) template:
  We are investigating elevated error rates for text generation calls in eu-west-1. Our on-call engineers are actively triaging and have initiated a controlled rollback to the last known-good runtime. We will provide an update within 15 minutes.

- 30-minute update example:
  Update at 14:32 UTC: The rollback has completed in eu-west-1. Error rates have decreased from 22% to 3% across affected endpoints. We are continuing to monitor and will follow up with a full RCA.

- Resolution example:
  The issue in eu-west-1 was caused by an inadvertent config change pushed to routing-proxy that increased request fanout. We reverted the change and scaled the runtime pool. A formal postmortem is scheduled and customers impacted are being contacted by CS.

Document ownership and maintenance

- Owner: eng-sre incident operations (document steward: Maya Patel)
- Review cadence: quarterly reviews and after every Sev 1/Sev 2 incident.

Related resources

- Incident command playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-command-playbook-2024
- Bridge operator manual: /confluence/eng-sre/bridge-operator-manual-2024
- Runbook repository: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-library

Notes and best practices

- Keep customer language factual and non-technical for external comms; internal channels should preserve technical evidence.
- Prefer incremental mitigations that are reversible over broad, irreversible changes.
- Timebox efforts: if an action is not producing measurable improvement in 10 minutes, switch strategy and escalate.

End of document
